We had originally planned to begin this session with the talk I gave yesterday,
building a new foundation for the Biodiversity Heritage Library, but
we did have the incredible opportunity to deliver that talk as part of

That meant that I could share BHL's transition story with the entire conference,
which was wonderful. But as I said, that talk was meant to set the
scene for this symposium and provide some context for the talks
that follow. So for anyone who wasn't there, and to give us a starting
point for today, here's a very short recap of yesterday's talk.
Over the past 18 months, BHL has moved
from being hosted administratively and technically by the Smithsonian
Institution to operating as an independent, globally
governed consortium. BHL now has a new financial home, a
new legal home, new technical hosting, strengthened governance, new
members and partners, and a major platform modernization effort underway.
2026 is both BHL's 20th anniversary and the beginning
of our completely new chapter. After an intense period of transition, we
now have the foundation, resources, and momentum to start
shaping what BHL becomes next. While we are on much
firmer ground than we were this time last year, our long-term future is not yet
secure, but that's why we're here.
We are really excited to hear new ideas, explore new partnerships,
and have the conversations that will shape BHL's future.
When we put the calls out for abstracts for this symposium, we knew that there
would be plenty to discuss, and we were really delighted by the range and the
quality of the abstracts we received.
Today, we'll hear eight fabulous talks across our two themed sessions.
So that first session, this one, is Reimagining BHL, the foundations,
partnerships, and future infrastructure.
We'll begin with Joe Miller, who'll take us back to the original vision for GBIF
and ask what that vision might mean today.
Then we'll hear from Sydney Jordan and Amanda Bozar about the University of South
Florida's new partnership with BHL and their work with archives,
digitized collections, and data extraction.
And then Harris Goo will introduce the Natural History Museum in London's
work connecting BHL with the Planetary Knowledge Base and transforming
biodiversity literature into structured machine actionable knowledge.
And finally, Nikki Nicholson from Kew will explore new possibilities for
semantic navigation in BHL, including ways of moving beyond
pages and volumes towards more meaningful units of work.
And then after the break, we'll return for our second session, "Transforming BHL:
Data Extraction, Semantic Navigation, and Future Interfaces," where
we'll explore how biodiversity literature can be transformed into richer,
more connected, and more usable knowledge from extracting structured data and
uncovering relationships to rethinking how people discover and interact with
BHL.
Yesterday, I described BHL as a living bridge.
We've put down some strong roots, but we are still building.
We don't know yet what exactly lies on the other side or what BHL will look like
when we get there. But I said yesterday that uncertainty is also what's
making this time so exciting. Today's symposium is really about
exploring what is on that other side, and I'm thrilled that you're all here to
explore it with us. We have, as David said, generous discussion time
built into both sessions, partly because my session was moved, so we have more
time than we expected. So really do please ask questions, challenge
ideas, and help us think about what BHL's next chapter could look
like. You can contribute either here in the room or through the Whova
app.
On behalf of the BHL community, thank you to our amazing presenters for
